hint.label: Vocabulary

atoms.text: The novel describes a future in which humans are divided into social castes, with Alphas at the top and Epsilons at the bottom. They are no longer born naturally; embryos are cultivated in labs instead. Embryos assigned to be in lower castes are cloned, so that a factory may be staffed with dozens of twins with no individuality. These embryos are manipulated according to the jobs they will fulfil in the future. Future miners in tropical areas, for example, are conditioned to hate the cold. Additionally, they are given less oxygen than higher-caste embryos and receive alcohol injections to stunt their development. As a result, Alphas and Betas, who are fed much more nutrients as embryos, are smarter and more physically capable than Gammas, Deltas and Epsilons.

instruction.text: Which consequences does this extreme use of biotechnology have? Assign them to matching book quotes.

atoms.a: 'Alpha children wear grey. They work much harder than we do, because they're so frightfully clever. [...] Oh no, I don't want to play with Delta children. And Epsilons are still worse. They're too stupid to be able to read or write. [...] I'm so glad I'm a Beta.'

'We also predestine and condition. We decant our babies as socialized human beings, as Alphas or Epsilons, as future sewage workers or future...' He was going to say future World Controllers, but correcting himself, said 'future Directors of Hatcheries' instead.

hint.text:

to decant – umgießen, umfüllen (hier: als Alternative zum Geborenwerden)
sewage – Abwasser
hatchery – Brutplatz (hier: Ort, an dem Embryos gezüchtet werden)

atoms.a: 'But in Epsilons,' said Mr Foster very justly, 'we don't need human intelligence.'

'Try to realize what it was like to have a viviparous mother. [...] Try to imagine what “living with one's family” meant.'
They tried; but obviously without the smallest success.
'And do you know what a “home” was?'
They shook their heads.
